facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4740.04; Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board (OCILB), Division of Industrial Compliance
facts.fact: Ohio has no statewide general contractor license. The Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board (OCILB) licenses only five commercial trade contractor types: HVAC, refrigeration, electrical, plumbing and hydronics. General building and residential contractor registration is handled by cities and counties.
facts.note: Trade list from ORC 4740.04(E) https://codes.ohio.gov/orc/section-4740.04 ; OCILB testing application states the licenses cover commercial work https://dam.assets.ohio.gov/image/upload/com.ohio.gov/DICO/OCILB/Testing_Application_-_OCILB.pdf

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4740.06(B); OCILB Testing Application
facts.fact: To sit for an Ohio OCILB contractor exam, an applicant must be at least 18 and have at least 5 years of experience as a tradesperson in that trade immediately before applying. Alternatives include being a currently registered Ohio professional engineer with 3 years of construction business experience in the trade, or 5 years as an Ohio government inspector in the trade.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4740.06(B)(4); OCILB Testing Application
facts.fact: Ohio OCILB licensed contractors must carry at least $500,000 of contractor liability insurance, held under one contracting company name.

facts.source: PSI Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (updated 2/7/2024)
facts.fact: Ohio OCILB applicants must pass both a Business and Law exam and a trade exam, given by PSI. The Business and Law exam is open book (NASCLA Contractor's Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Ohio 4th ed.), has 50 questions (5 unscored pretest), allows 2 hours and requires 70% to pass.

facts.source: PSI Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (updated 2/7/2024)
facts.fact: The Ohio electrical contractor trade exam is open book with 100 questions (10 unscored pretest), 4 hours and a 70% passing score; references include the 2023 NEC (or NEC Handbook) and Ugly's Electrical References 2023.

facts.source: PSI Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (updated 2/7/2024)
facts.fact: The Ohio plumbing contractor exam is open book with 100 questions in 4 hours and a 70% passing score, using the 2024 Ohio Plumbing Code and the 2024 International Fuel Gas Code. The HVAC exam is also 100 questions in 4 hours at 70%, based on the 2024 Ohio Mechanical Code and 2021 IFGC.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4740.06(G)
facts.fact: An Ohio OCILB candidate who fails may retake the exam no sooner than 60 days after the last attempt, and after five failed attempts must file a new application.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4740.04(G)(2)(a); Ohio Adm. Code 4101:16-1-08(C)
facts.fact: Ohio law requires OCILB licensees to complete 10 hours of continuing education per year. Licensees in the board's good-standing program may instead complete 8 hours for an annual renewal or 24 hours to renew for three years.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 1311.05
facts.fact: When an Ohio owner has recorded a notice of commencement, a subcontractor or supplier not in direct contract with the owner must serve a notice of furnishing within 21 days after first furnishing labor or materials. Late notice only protects work done in the 21 days before service and afterward; the rule does not apply to home construction contracts.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 1311.06(B)
facts.fact: An Ohio mechanics' lien affidavit must be filed with the county recorder within 60 days after the last work or materials for a one- or two-family dwelling or residential condominium unit, and within 75 days for other (commercial) projects.

An Ohio mechanics' lien stays in force for 6 years after the affidavit is filed. The owner can shorten this by serving a notice to commence suit; the lienholder then has 60 days after service to file suit or the lien becomes void.

facts.source: Ohio Rev. Code § 4113.61
facts.fact: Under Ohio's prompt pay law, a contractor must pay its subcontractors and suppliers within 10 calendar days after receiving payment from the owner (and pass down retainage within 10 days of receiving it), or owe 18% annual interest. The rule does not apply to single-, two- or three-family detached homes.

facts.source: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board (CIB) website
facts.fact: Oklahoma does not require a state license for general contracting. The Oklahoma Construction Industries Board (CIB) licenses electrical, mechanical and plumbing tradespeople and contractors, registers roofing contractors, and licenses building and home inspectors; general contractors should check with local jurisdictions for local requirements.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Become an Electrical Journeyman page; Electrical License Act (59 O.S.)
facts.fact: An Oklahoma unlimited electrical journeyman needs 8,000 verifiable hours as a registered apprentice (at least 4,000 in commercial/industrial work, up to 2,000 from classroom education); a residential journeyman needs 4,000 hours (up to 1,000 from education). Apprentice hours count only if the apprentice was registered with the CIB.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Become an Electrical Contractor page
facts.fact: An Oklahoma unlimited electrical contractor needs 12,000 verifiable hours of electrical construction experience, including 4,000 hours as a licensed unlimited journeyman and 6,000 commercial/industrial hours with a licensed electrical contractor. A residential electrical contractor needs 8,000 total hours including 4,000 as a journeyman.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Active Contractor Requirements page
facts.fact: To hold an active Oklahoma electrical, mechanical or plumbing contractor license, the licensee must file a $5,000 corporate surety bond in the license holder's name and carry at least $50,000 of commercial general liability insurance, with the CIB listed as certificate holder; letting insurance lapse makes the license inactive.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Roofing page (Roofing Contractor Registration Act)
facts.fact: Oklahoma roofing contractors must register with the CIB and carry general liability insurance of at least $500,000 for residential roofing, or at least $1,000,000 for a commercial roofing endorsement; commercial endorsement holders need 4 hours of continuing education every 36 months.

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Testing/Exam Information page and Electrical page
facts.fact: Oklahoma electrical, mechanical, plumbing and roofing exams are given by PSI after the CIB approves the application. A candidate who fails an electrical exam may retest 30 days after the previous test date.
facts.note: https://oklahoma.gov/cib/your-industry/testing-and-exam-information.html ; https://oklahoma.gov/cib/your-industry/electrical.html . Question counts and passing scores were not confirmed (PSI bulletin not reviewed).

facts.source: Oklahoma CIB, Electrical, Plumbing and Mechanical pages
facts.fact: Oklahoma electrical journeyman and contractor licenses renew every 36 months and require 12 hours of CE per cycle (6 hours of code updates plus 6 other approved hours). Plumbing and mechanical journeymen and contractors need 6 hours of CE within the 36 months before license expiration.

In Oklahoma, a contractor who contracted directly with the owner must file a lien statement with the county clerk within 4 months after last furnishing labor or materials. A subcontractor or supplier must file within 90 days after last furnishing.

An Oklahoma subcontractor or supplier must send a pre-lien notice to the original contractor and the owner no later than 75 days after the last date it supplied labor or materials. Notice is not required for claims under $10,000 total or on non-owner-occupied residential projects of four or fewer units, but it is required for owner-occupied homes.
facts.note: Read on Justia's 2025 Oklahoma Statutes https://law.justia.com/codes/oklahoma/title-42/section-42-142-6/ , which flags an amendment (Laws 2025, c. 486) effective January 1, 2026; confirm the current thresholds and timing on OSCN before relying on them.

facts.fact: A suit to enforce an Oklahoma mechanics' lien must be filed within one year from the date the lien was filed with the county clerk.

facts.source: ORS 701.021; Oregon Construction Contractors Board (CCB)
facts.fact: Oregon requires anyone who bids, offers or works for compensation as a contractor on improvements to real property to hold a license from the Construction Contractors Board (CCB); there is no minimum dollar threshold. The license must carry an endorsement matching the work, such as Residential General, Residential Specialty, Residential Limited, or Commercial General/Specialty Level 1 or 2.

facts.source: Oregon Construction Contractors Board, CCB License page
facts.fact: Before an Oregon CCB license is issued, the Responsible Managing Individual must complete 16 hours of approved pre-license training and pass an open-book PSI exam of 80 questions in 3 hours, scoring 70% (56 correct). The exam is based on the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management (2nd edition, as listed by the CCB); people who passed the NASCLA commercial exam skip the training but still take the Oregon exam.

facts.source: Oregon Construction Contractors Board, CCB License page
facts.fact: Oregon CCB bond amounts depend on the endorsement: $25,000 for Residential General, $20,000 Residential Specialty, $15,000 Residential Limited, $80,000 Commercial General Level 1, $55,000 Commercial Specialty Level 1, and $25,000 for Commercial Level 2 endorsements.

facts.source: Oregon Construction Contractors Board, CCB License page
facts.fact: Oregon CCB minimum liability insurance is $500,000 per occurrence for Residential General, $300,000 for Residential Specialty, $100,000 for Residential Limited, $2,000,000 aggregate for Commercial General Level 1, $1,000,000 aggregate for Commercial General Level 2 and Commercial Specialty Level 1, and $500,000 per occurrence for Commercial Specialty Level 2.

facts.source: Oregon Construction Contractors Board, CCB License and Continuing Education pages
facts.fact: Oregon CCB licenses renew every two years. Residential contractors need 3 hours of CCB laws/regulations/business practices plus 5 more hours if licensed 6+ years or 13 more hours if licensed under 6 years. Commercial Level 2 needs 32 hours, and Level 1 needs 16 to 80 hours depending on the number of key employees.

facts.source: Oregon Building Codes Division (BCD), Licensing FAQ
facts.fact: Oregon electrical and plumbing licenses (such as General Journeyman Electrician J, General Supervising Electrician S and Journeyman Plumber JP) are issued by the Building Codes Division, separate from the CCB license. Most BCD licenses renew on a three-year cycle, and Oregon has reciprocity agreements for the J, S and JP licenses.

An Oregon contractor that was not properly CCB-licensed when it bid or contracted and throughout the work generally cannot perfect a construction lien, file a CCB complaint, or sue or arbitrate for payment on that work, subject to narrow exceptions.
facts.note: Statute text via https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_701.131 (secondary host of the ORS); heading confirmed on oregonlegislature.gov ORS chapter 701.

facts.fact: On Oregon residential projects, suppliers, laborers and equipment renters not in direct contract with the owner must give the owner a notice of right to a lien. It protects only work or materials provided from 8 days (excluding weekends and holidays) before the notice was delivered or mailed; commercial improvements are exempt.

An Oregon construction lien must be recorded no later than 75 days after the claimant stops providing labor or materials or 75 days after completion of construction, whichever is earlier. A foreclosure suit must be filed within 120 days after the lien is recorded, and the claimant must give the owner and mortgagee written notice of intent to foreclose at least 10 days before filing suit.

On Oregon private construction contracts, retainage may not exceed 5% of the contract price of completed work. Late final and retainage payments accrue interest at 1% per month, and retainage on contracts over $500,000 must be held in an interest-bearing escrow account.
facts.note: Statute text via https://oregon.public.law/statutes/ors_701.420 (secondary host of the ORS).

facts.source: Home Improvement Consumer Protection Act (HICPA), 73 P.S. § 517.1 et seq.; Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General
facts.fact: Pennsylvania has no statewide general contractor license. Instead, contractors who perform home improvements must register with the Office of Attorney General under HICPA, unless they do less than $5,000 of home improvement work in a calendar year. Registration is not an endorsement of quality and there is no exam.
facts.note: AG HICPA instructions https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/HICPA-instructions.pdf ; AG contractor FAQ https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/?p=6380 . Exam: none mentioned in the AG materials.

facts.source: HICPA; Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, HICPA registration instructions
facts.fact: Pennsylvania home improvement contractors must show liability insurance of at least $50,000 for bodily injury and at least $50,000 for property damage when registering with the Attorney General.

facts.source: HICPA; Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, Contractor FAQ
facts.fact: Pennsylvania home improvement contractor registrations are valid for two years and must be renewed every two years.

facts.source: HICPA; Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, Contractor FAQ
facts.fact: Under Pennsylvania's HICPA, a home improvement contract over $500 must be in writing, signed by both the homeowner and contractor, and must state the total price, estimated start and completion dates and a description of the work. The homeowner has a 3-day right to cancel, and the contract can stay voidable if the statutory cancellation notice is not given.

Pennsylvania's HICPA limits deposits on home improvement contracts: a contractor generally may not take a deposit of more than one-third of the contract price plus the cost of special-order materials.
facts.note: The AG FAQ (https://www.attorneygeneral.gov/?p=6380) says a one-third down payment is generally appropriate but does not quote the cap; the exact contract-size trigger (commonly cited as contracts over $1,000) could not be confirmed on the statute text, which was not fetchable.

facts.source: Local licensing (e.g., City of Philadelphia, City of Pittsburgh, Allegheny County)
facts.fact: Pennsylvania does not issue statewide electrician, plumber or HVAC licenses; trade licensing is handled by municipalities and counties such as Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Allegheny County, so requirements vary by location.
facts.note: Consistent across secondary licensing guides, but no official state page stating this was found in this session.

facts.source: Pennsylvania Mechanics' Lien Law of 1963, 49 P.S. §§ 1301, 1501, 1502, 1701
facts.fact: In Pennsylvania, a lien claim must be at least $500 and must be filed with the court within 6 months after the claimant's last work; subcontractors must first give the owner formal written notice of intent to lien at least 30 days before filing. Notice of the filing must be served on the owner within 1 month, and the claim must be enforced within 2 years of filing.
facts.note: From a secondary legal compendium https://www.alfainternational.com/compendium/construction/pennsylvania/ ; the PA legislature statute site was not reachable to confirm.

facts.source: 49 P.S. § 1501.3 (State Construction Notices Directory)
facts.fact: On Pennsylvania projects over $1,500,000 where the owner files a notice of commencement in the State Construction Notices Directory, subcontractors and suppliers must file a notice of furnishing within 45 days after first providing labor or materials to keep lien rights.
facts.note: From secondary source https://www.alfainternational.com/compendium/construction/pennsylvania/ ; not confirmed on the statute.

facts.source: Contractor and Subcontractor Payment Act (CASPA), 73 P.S. § 507
facts.fact: Under Pennsylvania's CASPA, a contractor must pay its subcontractor the amount received for the sub's work within 14 days after receiving each progress or final payment (or 14 days after the sub's invoice, if later). Late payments carry interest, and wrongful withholding can bring a 1% per month penalty plus attorney fees.
facts.note: From secondary source https://www.alfainternational.com/compendium/construction/pennsylvania/ ; statute not fetchable this session.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 5-65; Rhode Island Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB)
facts.fact: Rhode Island contractors must register with the Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB) rather than obtain a general contractor license. Applicants must complete a state-approved 5-hour pre-registration course (contractors working only on commercial structures are exempt); no exam is required and reciprocity is not available for this registration.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-65-7; CRLB application page
facts.fact: Rhode Island registered contractors must carry liability and property damage insurance with at least a $500,000 combined single limit, plus workers' compensation if they have employees, and must show proof at registration and each renewal. A lapse in insurance invalidates the registration.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 5-65.4 (enacted July 2, 2025); CRLB Residential Contractor Licensing page
facts.fact: Starting January 1, 2028, Rhode Island will require a license (Home Builder License or Structural Remodeler License) to build new homes or structurally remodel existing residential buildings. The new license does not apply to nonstructural home improvements or commercial construction, and the implementing rules (440-RICR-10-00-7) were still in proposed form as of late 2026.

facts.source: Rhode Island CRLB home page
facts.fact: Besides registering contractors, the Rhode Island CRLB issues licenses for commercial roofers, home inspectors, underground utility contractors, water filtration installers, well drillers and pump installers.

facts.source: Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training (DLT), Professional Regulation
facts.fact: Rhode Island trade licenses are issued by the Department of Labor and Training's Professional Regulation unit, through the Board of Examiners of Electricians, the Board of Examiners of Plumbers and the Mechanical Board, which examines pipefitters, refrigeration technicians, sheet metal workers and sprinkler fitters.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws § 5-6-8
facts.fact: In Rhode Island, a Certificate A lets a person or company do business as an electrical contractor, but holding it does not by itself let the holder personally perform electrical installation work; the work must be done by licensed electricians.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-28-4(a)
facts.fact: To claim a Rhode Island mechanics' lien, the claimant must mail a notice of intention to the owner and record it in the land evidence records within 200 days after doing the work or furnishing the materials.

facts.source: R.I. Gen. Laws § 34-28-10
facts.fact: A Rhode Island lien claimant must file a complaint to enforce the lien, together with a lis pendens notice, within 40 days after recording the notice of intention; otherwise the lien is lost for work done before the 200-day period.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-30; South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board (LLR) 2023 Legislative Update
facts.fact: South Carolina requires a General Contractor's or Mechanical Contractor's license from the Contractor's Licensing Board (part of the Department of Labor, Licensing and Regulation) for commercial work when the total cost of construction is more than $10,000. The threshold was raised from $5,000 by 2023 legislation.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. Title 40, Ch. 59; South Carolina Residential Builders Commission
facts.fact: In South Carolina, residential construction (buildings no more than three floors high and apartment buildings of no more than 16 units) costing more than $5,000 requires a Residential Builder license from the Residential Builders Commission. Exam candidates take a technical portion and a Business Management and Law portion; the technical portion can be waived for those who passed the NASCLA Commercial General Building exam within the past 3 years.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-260; SC Contractor's Licensing Board 2023 Legislative Update
facts.fact: South Carolina general contractor license groups set bid and job limits: Group 1 up to $100,000, Group 2 up to $400,000, Group 3 up to $1,000,000, Group 4 up to $3,000,000 and Group 5 unlimited. Each group requires minimum working capital or net worth (for example, Group 1 needs $10,000 working capital or $20,000 net worth).

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-260; SC Contractor's Licensing Board 2023 Legislative Update
facts.fact: South Carolina mechanical contractor license groups (covering classifications such as plumbing, air conditioning, heating and electrical) have job limits of $35,000 (Group 1), $100,000 (Group 2), $200,000 (Group 3), $400,000 (Group 4) and unlimited (Group 5).

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-262; SC Contractor's Licensing Board 2023 Legislative Update
facts.fact: A South Carolina contractor can qualify for a license group by meeting either the net worth or the working capital requirement, or by posting a surety bond in place of a financial statement. Since 2023, the bond equals the net worth required for the group (for example, $20,000 for general contractor Group 1 and $350,000 for Group 5).

facts.source: PSI South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (updated 8/27/2026)
facts.fact: South Carolina commercial contractor exams are given by PSI and are open book. The Business Management and Law exam has 50 questions, requires 35 correct and allows 125 minutes, using the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management (SC Commercial 9th ed.). The Building Contractor technical exam has 80 questions, 56 correct to pass, 5 hours.
keywords: South Carolina business and law exam

facts.source: PSI South Carolina Contractor's Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (updated 8/27/2026)
facts.fact: South Carolina mechanical trade exams through PSI: Electrician 80 questions, 56 correct, 5 hours (2020 NEC); Plumber 80 questions, 56 correct, 4 hours (2021 IPC); Air Conditioning 80 questions, 56 correct, 4 hours (2021 IMC, ACCA Manuals). The NASCLA accredited electrical contractor exam is accepted as an alternative.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-250; SC Contractor's Licensing Board 2023 Legislative Update
facts.fact: South Carolina contractor licenses renew every two years: general contractor licenses expire October 31 of even-numbered years and mechanical contractor licenses October 31 of odd-numbered years. A lapsed license may be renewed within 90 days of expiration with late fees.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. § 40-11-370(C)
facts.fact: An entity that performs South Carolina work requiring a contractor's license without a valid license cannot bring a lawsuit, at law or in equity, to enforce the contract.

A South Carolina mechanics' lien is dissolved unless the claimant serves the owner and files a sworn statement of account (certificate of lien) within 90 days after last furnishing labor or materials, and files suit with a notice of pendency within 6 months after last furnishing.

facts.source: S.C. Code Ann. §§ 29-6-30, 29-6-50 (prompt payment)
facts.fact: Under South Carolina's prompt payment law for private projects, an owner must pay an undisputed pay request within 21 days of receipt, and a contractor must pay its subcontractor within 7 days of receiving payment for the sub's work. Late payments carry interest of 1% per month if the payee gave notice of this law when requesting payment; retainage must be a reasonable amount but no fixed cap is set.

facts.source: South Dakota licensing structure (secondary guides); local building departments
facts.fact: South Dakota does not issue a statewide general contractor or HVAC license; general contractors are regulated locally by cities and counties, while electricians and plumbers are licensed by state commissions.
facts.note: Commonly reported by licensing guides; no official state page explicitly stating the absence of a GC license was found this session. Electrical and plumbing commissions confirmed on dlr.sd.gov.

facts.source: SDCL ch. 10-46A; South Dakota Department of Revenue, Contractor's Excise Tax page
facts.fact: Anyone in South Dakota who contracts for construction services or builds, installs or repairs fixtures attached to real property must hold a South Dakota contractor's excise tax license. The contractor's excise tax is 2% of gross receipts on prime contractors, and the department recommends getting a prime contractor's exemption certificate before work starts so subcontractors are not treated as primes.

facts.source: South Dakota State Electrical Commission (Dept. of Labor & Regulation), Licensing page
facts.fact: The South Dakota State Electrical Commission licenses all electricians in the state, including apprentices, journeymen, electrical contractors and Class B electricians. The journeyman exam requires 4 years (8,000 hours) as a licensed apprentice under an electrical contractor; the contractor exam requires 2 more years (4,000 hours) as a licensed journeyman, including at least 2,000 commercial hours.

facts.source: South Dakota State Electrical Commission home page
facts.fact: Since December 2, 2024, all South Dakota electrical licensing exams are based on the 2023 National Electrical Code.

facts.source: SDCL ch. 36-16; South Dakota State Electrical Commission, Undertaking & Insurance page
facts.fact: South Dakota electrical contractors and Class B electricians must file a $10,000 undertaking (bond) and keep public liability insurance of at least $100,000 per occurrence and $300,000 aggregate for bodily injury, with at least $25,000 per occurrence for property damage (or a $300,000 combined single limit).

facts.source: South Dakota State Electrical Commission, Licensing and Continuing Education pages; ARSD 20:44:17:02
facts.fact: South Dakota electrical licenses renew every two years, and licensees need 16 hours of continuing education per cycle (at least 8 on the National Electrical Code); no more than 8 hours may come from pre-approved online courses.

facts.source: South Dakota State Plumbing Commission, Licensing page
facts.fact: South Dakota plumbers are licensed by the State Plumbing Commission. A plumber (journeyman) needs 4 years as an apprentice plumber, and a plumbing contractor needs 6 years of experience (at least 2 as a contractor or plumber), with at least 1,900 hours worked in each qualifying year. Plumbing licenses expire every December 31 and require continuing education to renew.

A South Dakota mechanics' lien is lost unless the claim statement is filed with the county register of deeds within 120 days after the last work or the last item furnished. Before filing, the claimant must mail a copy of the lien statement to the owner by registered or certified mail and attach the mailing receipt.
A South Dakota property owner (or contractor) can serve a written demand on a lien claimant to start suit; the claimant must then sue within 30 days or the lien is forfeited.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-102(4)(A)(i); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: In Tennessee, anyone who bids, offers a price on, or performs a construction project whose total cost is $25,000 or more (materials and labor) must hold a contractor's license from the Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, part of the Department of Commerce & Insurance. The license must be in hand before bidding or negotiating, not just before starting work.
facts.note: Statute text on law.justia.com (2025 Tenn. Code) https://law.justia.com/codes/tennessee/title-62/chapter-6/part-1/section-62-6-102/ ; board page https://www.tn.gov/commerce/regboards/contractors/license/get/contractor.html

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-102(4)(A)(ii) and (5); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: Tennessee subcontractors need their own contractor's license when their portion of the job reaches the threshold: electrical, mechanical, plumbing, HVAC and roofing subcontractors at $25,000 or more, and masonry contractors (LMC classification) only when the masonry portion exceeds $100,000 including materials and labor.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-102(4)(A)(iii)
facts.fact: When a Tennessee project costs more than $25,000, construction managers of any kind (including residential construction managers and construction consultants, and architects or engineers performing contractor-type services beyond normal design services) are also treated as contractors and must be licensed.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Contractor license requirements page
facts.fact: Tennessee building classifications include BC-A (residential), BC-B (commercial), BC-C (industrial), BC (combined residential/commercial/industrial), BC-B,C (commercial/industrial) and BC-A,b(sm) (residential plus small commercial, for commercial projects under $750,000). Mechanical classifications are CMC (full mechanical: plumbing and HVAC), CMC-A (plumbing), CMC-C (HVAC/refrigeration) and CMC-D (fire sprinkler); CE is electrical.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-111(c)-(d)
facts.fact: A Tennessee license in one major classification does not let a contractor perform work of $25,000 or more in a different classification; the contractor must also be licensed in that other classification (for example, a BC-A residential contractor cannot do a $25,000+ electrical job without the CE classification).

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-103(b)
facts.fact: An unlicensed contractor in Tennessee who performs work requiring a license can recover in court only actual documented expenses proven by clear and convincing evidence; profit on the job is not recoverable.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-103(c)
facts.fact: Under Tennessee law, no mechanics' lien under Title 66, Chapter 11 is available to a person who performed construction in violation of the contractor licensing law, so an unlicensed contractor cannot lien the property.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Rule 0680-01-.13; Contractor license requirements page
facts.fact: Every Tennessee contractor's license carries a monetary limit, the largest single project the contractor may take on. It is calculated as 10 times the lesser of working capital or net worth (for example, a $150,000 limit requires at least $15,000 of both); with $10,000 working capital and $200,000 net worth, the limit is $100,000.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Contractor license requirements page
facts.fact: To get an unlimited monetary limit in Tennessee, the contractor needs at least $300,000 in both working capital and net worth (plus the required experience). Each project gets a 10% tolerance above the limit, there is no cap on the number of projects, and a job cannot be split into phases to stay under the limit.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-111(b)(3)-(4); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: A Tennessee license applicant must submit a financial statement prepared under GAAP by a licensed CPA or LPA: a reviewed or audited statement for a monetary limit of $3,000,000 or less, and an audited statement for a limit above $3,000,000. The board says the statement must be less than 12 months old when the application is filed.
facts.note: Statute https://law.justia.com/codes/tennessee/title-62/chapter-6/part-1/section-62-6-111/ and board page https://www.tn.gov/commerce/regboards/contractors/license/get/contractor.html . An older board Financial Resources PDF still shows a $1,500,000 cut-off, which is outdated for initial applications.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Renewal, Retirement and Revisions page
facts.fact: At renewal, a Tennessee contractor with a monetary limit of $1,500,000 or less may submit a self-prepared financial statement, while a limit above $1,500,000 requires at least a CPA-compiled statement; the numbers must still support the current monetary limit.
facts.note: https://tn.gov/commerce/regboards/contractor/contractors-renewal-retirement-and-revisions.html . A separate board Financial Resources PDF says a CPA-reviewed statement is acceptable above $1.5M at renewal; reviewer may want to confirm the current wording.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Contractor license requirements page (Restricted Residential Limited License)
facts.fact: Tennessee offers a restricted residential limited license (BC-A/r) for residential contractors who complete an approved course at a Tennessee community college or vocational school instead of taking the BC-A trade exam and the Business and Law exam. It is limited to projects under $125,000, has no 10% tolerance, and raising the limit requires passing the exams and a reviewed financial statement.
facts.note: https://www.tn.gov/commerce/regboards/contractors/license/get/contractor.html (page labels it both BA-A/r and BC-A/r; BC-A/r is the designation used elsewhere by the board).

facts.source: PSI Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 4/15/2026); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: Every Tennessee contractor license applicant must pass the Business and Law exam, given by PSI. It is open book using the NASCLA Contractors' Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Tennessee Edition (4th ed.), has 50 questions, allows 140 minutes, and requires 37 correct answers (a 73% passing score).

facts.source: PSI Tennessee Contractors Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 4/15/2026), Business and Law content outline
facts.fact: The 50-question Tennessee Business and Law exam covers licensing requirements (5), estimating and bidding (7), business organization and financial management (7), tax laws (5), labor laws (5), project management and lien law (6), contracts (6), risk management (4), and environmental and safety (5).

facts.source: PSI Tennessee Contractors Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 4/15/2026)
facts.fact: The Tennessee BC-A residential trade exam is open book with 100 questions in 300 minutes and a 73% passing score (73 correct); main references include the 2021 International Residential Code and OSHA 29 CFR 1926. The BC-B commercial exam is also 100 questions in 300 minutes at 73%, based on the 2021 International Building Code and OSHA 1926.

facts.source: PSI Tennessee Contractors Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 4/15/2026)
facts.fact: Tennessee mechanical trade exams are open book with a 73% passing score: CMC-C HVAC/Refrigeration has 100 questions in 260 minutes, CMC-A Mechanical Plumbing has 110 questions in 295 minutes, and CMC Full Mechanical has 120 questions in 325 minutes. References include the 2021 IMC, IPC and IFGC plus Manual J.

facts.source: PSI Tennessee Contractors Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 4/15/2026)
facts.fact: The Tennessee CE (electrical contractor) exam is open book with 100 questions, 260 minutes and a 73% passing score (73 correct). Its references include the 2017 NEC (NFPA 70) and NEC Handbook, NFPA 70E 2017, the 2021 IBC, OSHA 1926 and Ugly's Electrical References.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-111(l); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: Tennessee CMC-A (plumbing) and CMC (full mechanical) applicants must get Board pre-approval before testing and must show three years of plumbing experience or an engineering degree in plumbing or a mechanical field.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors; PSI Tennessee bulletin (NASCLA section)
facts.fact: Tennessee accepts the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors (115 questions, 81 correct to pass, 330 minutes) in place of its own commercial trade exam. Reciprocal agreements with other states only waive the trade exam; they do not let a contractor use another state's license in Tennessee, so the Business and Law exam and a Tennessee license are still required.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-111(a)(1)(A); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
facts.fact: Tennessee initial and renewal applicants must file an affidavit that they carry general liability insurance and workers' compensation insurance, and must include proof of current workers' compensation coverage (or proof of exemption); without it the applicant is ineligible. The board sets general liability amounts based on the monetary limit.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Contractor license requirements page and Financial Resources guide
facts.fact: When a Tennessee applicant's financial statement is deficient, the board may require an indemnity: a personal or parent-company guaranty, or a board-format contractor's bond of $500,000 ($1,000,000 for an unlimited monetary limit). A line of credit in the board's format can also be added to working capital.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Renewal Resource and Renewal page
facts.fact: Tennessee contractor licenses are issued for two years and expire on the last day of the month in which they were originally issued. There is no grace period to keep contracting after expiration; a license can be renewed late (with penalties) within 12 months, after which a new application is required.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Residential Continuing Education FAQ (Public Chapter 186)
facts.fact: Tennessee residential contractors with a BC-A, BC-A/r or BC-A,b(sm) license originally issued after January 1, 2009 must complete 8 hours of board-approved Residential Continuing Education within the two years before each renewal. The qualifying agent takes the courses; commercial-only licenses (BC, BC-B) are exempt unless they include BC-A.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 62-6-501, 62-6-516; Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Home Improvement page
facts.fact: A Tennessee Home Improvement license is required for residential remodeling (1 to 4 dwelling units) priced over $3,000 and under $25,000, but only in counties that adopted the law: Bradley, Davidson, Hamilton, Haywood, Knox, Marion, Robertson, Rutherford and Shelby. At $25,000 and above a contractor's license is needed instead.
facts.note: https://tn.gov/commerce/regboards/hi/county-information-adopting-the-home-improvement-law.html ; https://tn.gov/commerce/regboards/hi/home-improvement-licensing-requirements.html ; statute https://law.justia.com/codes/tennessee/title-62/chapter-6/part-5/section-62-6-501/ . County list can change as counties opt in.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Other Licenses Regulated and Home Improvement pages
facts.fact: A Tennessee contractor who already holds a BC-A, BC or BC-B classification does not need a separate Home Improvement license. A Home Improvement license does not cover electrical, plumbing or HVAC work, which require the appropriate state limited license or local trade license, and the license number must appear in advertising.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 62-6-102(6); Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, LLE License Process
facts.fact: A Tennessee Limited Licensed Electrician (LLE) license covers electrical jobs where the total electrical work is under $25,000, in areas without their own local electrical licensing and inspection (where the State Fire Marshal inspects). Applicants must pass the LLE trade exam through PSI, the license runs two years, jobs cannot be split to stay under $25,000, and contractors holding a CE classification are exempt.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, LLP License Process
facts.fact: A Tennessee Limited Licensed Plumber (LLP) may do plumbing jobs where total plumbing is under $25,000; $25,000 or more requires a contractor's license with the CMC-A classification. Applicants need one year of plumbing experience (or a prior local Tennessee plumbing license) and must pass a 40-question PSI plumbing exam; the license is issued for two years and local permits and local requirements still apply.

facts.source: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors, Other Licenses Regulated page
facts.fact: In Tennessee, HVAC jobs under $25,000 in State Fire Marshal inspection areas require an LLE to pull permits, while HVAC work of $25,000 or more (as prime or subcontractor) requires a contractor's license with the CMC or CMC-C classification. Local codes offices may have their own HVAC licensing.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-106
facts.fact: A Tennessee prime contractor's (direct-with-owner) mechanics' lien lasts for one year after the improvement is completed or abandoned, and continues until a final decision in any enforcement suit properly filed within that one year.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-112(a)-(b)
facts.fact: A Tennessee lienor who has not recorded its contract must record a sworn statement of the amount owed and a property description with the county register of deeds within 90 days after the improvement is completed or abandoned. Abandonment means a 90-day stop in work with intent to quit permanently or indefinitely.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-145
facts.fact: On Tennessee projects other than 1-to-4-family residential, a remote contractor (sub or supplier not in contract with the owner) must serve a notice of nonpayment on the owner and the prime contractor within 90 days of the last day of each month in which it provided unpaid work or materials. Failing to serve it means losing the right to a lien (the notice is not required for retainage).

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-115
facts.fact: A Tennessee remote contractor must serve a written notice of lien on the owner within the 90-day recording period after completion or abandonment. Its lien then lasts 90 days from the date that notice is served, and a suit to enforce must be filed within those 90 days.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-146
facts.fact: On owner-occupied residential property in Tennessee (a one-unit home the owner lives in or plans to live in, or a 2-4 unit building where the owner lives in one unit), mechanics' lien rights exist only for the prime contractor, so subcontractors and suppliers generally cannot lien.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-11-143
facts.fact: A Tennessee owner may record a notice of completion. A contractor claiming a lien that has not already recorded its contract or sworn statement must then serve written notice of its claim within 10 days of recording for 1-to-4-family residential work, or within 30 days for other projects, or its lien rights expire. A notice of completion recorded before work is finished is void.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-34-103
facts.fact: Tennessee caps retainage at 5% of the contract amount. The owner must release retainage within 90 days after completion of the work or substantial completion, whichever comes first, and each contractor must pass retainage down to its subcontractors within 10 days of receiving it.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-34-104
facts.fact: On Tennessee projects where the prime contract is $500,000 or more, any retainage withheld must be deposited in a separate, interest-bearing escrow account with a third party. A party that fails to do so owes $300 per day in damages, and the requirement cannot be waived by contract.

facts.source: Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 66-34-302, 66-34-601 (Prompt Pay Act)
facts.fact: Under the Tennessee Prompt Pay Act, a prime contractor must pay a subcontractor within 30 days after the sub timely submits its payment application (per the contract's schedule). Late payments earn the interest rate stated in the contract, or 1.5% per month if the contract is silent.

facts.source: Texas licensing structure; Texas Residential Construction Commission abolished 2009 (sunset)
facts.fact: Texas has no statewide general contractor or residential builder license; the former Texas Residential Construction Commission was abolished in 2009. Some cities require local registration, while electricians and air conditioning contractors are licensed by TDLR and plumbers by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners.
facts.note: Widely reported, but no official state page explicitly stating the absence of a GC license was retrieved this session. TDLR and TSBPE roles confirmed on https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/electricians/elec.htm , https://www.tdlr.texas.gov/acr/acr.htm and https://tsbpe.texas.gov/

facts.source: Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation (TDLR), Electricians program; Tex. Occ. Code ch. 1305
facts.fact: In Texas, anyone doing non-exempt electrical work must hold a TDLR license and perform the work through a licensed electrical contractor. Individual licenses include apprentice, residential wireman, journeyman, journeyman industrial, maintenance and master electrician; electrical contractor is a separate business license.

A Texas journeyman electrician needs at least 8,000 hours of on-the-job training under a master electrician and must pass the journeyman exam. A master electrician needs at least 12,000 hours of on-the-job training under a master electrician, must have held a journeyman license for at least 2 years, and must pass the master exam.
facts.note: Statute text via https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._occ._code_section_1305.155 and https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._occ._code_section_1305.153 (reproduction of the Texas Occupations Code).

facts.source: Tex. Occ. Code § 1305.159
facts.fact: A Texas electrical contractor license requires the applicant to be, or employ, a licensed master electrician, to show financial responsibility (insurance) as TDLR prescribes, and to carry workers' compensation or properly elect not to. A master electrician may be assigned to only one electrical contractor unless he or she owns more than 50% of the business.
facts.note: https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._occ._code_section_1305.159 . Insurance dollar amounts are set by TDLR rule and were not confirmed this session.

facts.source: TDLR Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors program, Apply for a Contractor License page; Tex. Occ. Code ch. 1302
facts.fact: Texas air conditioning and refrigeration contractors are licensed by TDLR. A Class A license covers any size unit, while Class B is limited to cooling systems of 25 tons or less and heating systems of 1.5 million BTU/hour or less. Applicants need 48 months of supervised experience in the past 72 months (or a technician certification held 12 months plus 36 months of experience in the past 48 months) and must pass the exam within one year of applying.

facts.source: TDLR Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors program, Apply for a Contractor License page
facts.fact: Texas ACR contractors must carry commercial general liability insurance: Class A needs $300,000 per occurrence, $600,000 aggregate, and $300,000 products/completed operations; Class B needs $100,000 per occurrence, $200,000 aggregate and $100,000 products/completed operations.

facts.source: TDLR ACR Continuing Education Requirements page
facts.fact: Texas ACR contractors must complete 8 hours of continuing education to renew, including 1 hour on Texas law and the rules governing licensee conduct.

facts.source: Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners (TSBPE), Journeyman and Responsible Master Plumber pages
facts.fact: Texas plumbers are licensed by the Texas State Board of Plumbing Examiners (TSBPE), with tiers of Tradesman Plumber-Limited, Journeyman, Master and Responsible Master Plumber. A journeyman needs at least 8,000 hours of plumbing experience plus a TSBPE-approved 48-hour course or a registered apprenticeship; a Responsible Master Plumber must hold a Texas master license and carry $300,000 of commercial liability insurance.

facts.source: Tex. Prop. Code § 53.056(a-1)
facts.fact: A Texas subcontractor or supplier (derivative claimant) must send notice of its unpaid claim to the owner and the original contractor by the 15th day of the third month after the month the labor or materials were provided; on residential construction projects the deadline is the 15th day of the second month.
facts.note: Statute text via https://texas.public.law/statutes/tex._prop._code_section_53.056 (reflects the 2022 lien law overhaul).

facts.fact: A Texas lien affidavit must be filed with the county clerk by the 15th day of the fourth month after the month the original contract work was completed, terminated or abandoned (15th day of the third month for residential construction). A suit to foreclose must be filed by the first anniversary of the last day the lien affidavit could have been filed, extendable to two years by written agreement with the owner.

facts.source: Tex. Prop. Code § 53.101
facts.fact: A Texas owner must withhold (reserve) 10% of the contract price during the work and for 30 days after the work is completed, to protect subcontractors and suppliers who timely perfect liens.

facts.source: Tex. Prop. Code §§ 28.002, 28.004 (Prompt Payment to Contractors and Subcontractors)
facts.fact: Under Texas's prompt pay law, an owner must pay a contractor within 35 days after receiving a written payment request, and the contractor must pay each subcontractor within 7 days after receiving the owner's payment. Unpaid amounts bear interest at 1.5% per month.

facts.source: Utah Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL), General Contractor application page; Utah Code Title 58, Ch. 55
facts.fact: Utah contractors are licensed by the Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL) in the Department of Commerce. General contractor classifications are B100 (General Building), R100 (Residential and Small Commercial) and E100 (General Engineering); specialty contractors hold separate S-classifications.

facts.source: Utah DOPL, General Contractor application page and Contracting FAQ
facts.fact: A Utah B100, R100 or E100 general contractor license requires at least 2 years (4,000 hours) of paid construction experience, self-certified. Alternatives include 2 years as a qualifier on a Utah contractor license, a construction management degree, a Utah PE license, or passing the NASCLA Accredited Examination for Commercial General Building Contractors. Specialty contractor licenses require no experience.

facts.source: Utah DOPL, General Contractor application page and Contracting Exam Information page
facts.fact: Utah general contractor (B100, R100, E100) applicants, and electrical (E200/E201) and plumbing (P200/P201) contractors, must pass the Utah Business and Law exam, now offered in English and Spanish. It can be waived with one year of active licensed experience in another state in a similar scope, or for those who were qualifiers before May 9, 2017.
facts.note: https://commerce.utah.gov/dopl/contracting/apply-for-a-license/general-contractor/ ; https://dopl.utah.gov/contracting/exam-information/ . Question count/passing score are in the exam handbook, not reviewed.

facts.source: Utah DOPL, Specialty Contractor License application page
facts.fact: Utah specialty contractor applicants (and general contractors, who must meet all specialty requirements too) must complete a 25-hour pre-licensure course through an approved provider such as ABC, UHBA or AGC.

facts.source: Utah DOPL, Specialty Contractor License application page
facts.fact: Utah contractor applicants must carry general liability insurance of at least $1,000,000 per incident and $2,000,000 total, with DOPL as certificate holder, and must have workers' compensation coverage for employees (or a Labor Commission waiver if they have none). Every active license must maintain liability insurance and financial responsibility.
facts.note: https://commerce.utah.gov/dopl/contracting/apply-for-a-license/specialty-contractor-license/ ; https://commerce.utah.gov/dopl/contracting/frequently-asked-questions/ . These limits are higher than figures in many older guides ($100,000/$300,000).

facts.source: Utah DOPL, General Contractor application page
facts.fact: In Utah, electrical contractor classifications (E200 General Electrical, E201 Residential Electrical) must have a Master Electrician as qualifier, and plumbing contractor classifications (P200 General Plumbing, P201 Residential Plumbing) must have a Master Plumber as qualifier.

facts.source: Utah DOPL, Contracting FAQ and Continuing Education page; Utah Admin. Code R156-55a
facts.fact: Utah contractor licenses renew every two years and all expire on November 30 of each odd-numbered year. Licensees must complete 6 hours of approved continuing education per licensing period, at least 3 of them core hours, with no more than 3 hours online.

facts.source: Utah Code § 38-1a-501
facts.fact: In Utah, anyone who wants lien rights must file a preliminary notice with the State Construction Registry no later than 20 days after first providing construction work. A late notice protects only work done starting 5 days after it is filed, and a notice filed more than 10 days after a notice of completion has no effect.

A Utah notice of construction lien must be recorded within 180 days after final completion of the original contract if no notice of completion is filed, or within 90 days after a notice of completion is filed (but no later than 180 days after final completion). A copy goes to the owner within 30 days, and an action to enforce the lien must be filed within 180 days after the lien is filed.
facts.note: Recording deadlines confirmed on https://le.utah.gov/xcode/Title38/Chapter1A/C38-1a-P5_1800010118000101.pdf ; 180-day enforcement deadline (38-1a-701) per title insurer summary https://media.fntic.com/ncs/mechanicslienbystate/52/

facts.source: Utah Code § 13-8-5
facts.fact: On Utah construction contracts (private and public, nonresidential), retention may not exceed 5% of each payment or of the total contract price, and must be released with interest within 45 days after the later of final acceptance/certificate of occupancy and related billing events. Knowingly and wrongfully withholding retention brings a 2% per month charge.
facts.note: https://le.utah.gov/xcode/Title13/Chapter8/C13-8-S5_2023022720230227.pdf (this version is superseded 1/1/2027, so recheck after that date).

facts.source: 26 V.S.A. ch. 106, § 5501 (Act 182); Vermont Office of Professional Regulation (OPR)
facts.fact: Vermont has no statewide general contractor license, but since April 1, 2023 residential contractors must register with the Office of Professional Regulation (Secretary of State) before contracting for residential work worth more than $10,000, including labor and materials.
facts.note: https://sos.vermont.gov/residential-contractors/ ; OPR 2024 regulatory status report to the Legislature https://legislature.vermont.gov/assets/Legislative-Reports/Office-of-Professional-Regulation-2024-Residential-Contractors-Regulatory-Status-Report.pdf

facts.source: 26 V.S.A. § 5510(b); Vermont OPR Residential Contractors page
facts.fact: Vermont residential contractor registration is not a judgment of work quality: OPR disciplines unlawful and unprofessional conduct by registrants but does not seek money damages, mediate disputes or inspect construction. Act 182 also created voluntary certifications (such as OSHA construction safety and energy-efficient building methods).

facts.source: 26 V.S.A. ch. 15; Vermont Department of Public Safety, Division of Fire Safety, Electrical license application
facts.fact: Vermont electricians are licensed by the Electrical Licensing Board within the Department of Public Safety's Division of Fire Safety, with Master, Journeyman and Specialist classifications. Licenses are issued for 3 years, a Master applicant may qualify after holding a Vermont Journeyman license for 2 years, and Specialist licenses require a recognized training program plus one year (2,000 hours) of experience per specialty.

facts.source: Vermont Division of Fire Safety, Plumbing and Electrical licensing pages
facts.fact: Vermont plumbers are licensed through the Plumbers Examining Board in the Division of Fire Safety. Both plumbing and electrical applicants and renewals after July 1, 2021 must complete the state energy educational module and submit the completion certificate.

In Vermont, a subcontractor or supplier not hired by the owner must give the owner written notice that it will claim a lien (including the payment due date, if known); the lien covers only the contract balance unpaid when the owner gets the notice. A lien lapses unless notice is filed with the town clerk within 180 days after payment became due for the last labor or materials.

A Vermont lien claimant must start a court action to enforce the lien (and may attach the property) within 180 days after filing the lien memorandum, or within 180 days after payment becomes due if it was not yet due at filing.

facts.source: 9 V.S.A. §§ 4002, 4003 (Prompt Pay Act)
facts.fact: Under Vermont's Prompt Pay Act, unless agreed otherwise, an owner must pay a contractor 20 days after the end of the billing period or 20 days after receiving the invoice, whichever is later, and a contractor must pay its subcontractor 7 days after receiving payment (or after the sub's invoice, if later). Late payments bear interest at the statutory judgment rate under 12 V.S.A. § 2903(b).

Vermont retainage due at final completion must be paid within 30 days after final acceptance of the work, and the contractor must pay each subcontractor its share within 7 days after receiving the retainage, regardless of any contrary agreement. The statute does not set a maximum retainage percentage.

facts.source: Va. Code § 54.1-1100 (as amended 2025, cc. 127, 133); Virginia Board for Contractors (DPOR)
facts.fact: Virginia contractors are licensed by the Board for Contractors (Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation) in three classes. As amended in 2025: Class C covers single jobs over $1,000 but under $30,000 with under $250,000 per 12 months; Class B covers single jobs of $30,000 to under $150,000 or $250,000 to under $1 million per 12 months; Class A covers single jobs of $150,000 or more or $1 million or more per 12 months.
facts.note: https://law.lis.virginia.gov/vacode/title54.1/chapter11/section54.1-1100/ . These 2025 thresholds replace the older $10,000/$120,000 and $150,000/$750,000 figures still printed in many study guides.

facts.source: 18VAC50-22-40, -50, -60 (Board for Contractors regulations)
facts.fact: Virginia license qualifiers need experience in the classification: 1 year for Class C, 3 years for Class B and 5 years for Class A. For Class A and B, the designated employee must pass a board-approved exam, and for all classes the designated employee or a member of responsible management must complete a board-approved basic business course.

A Virginia Class A contractor firm must show net worth or equity of $45,000, and a Class B firm $15,000 (excluding property held as tenants by the entirety). Either class may instead post a $50,000 surety bond on the board's form.

facts.source: 18VAC50-30 (Individual License and Certification Regulations); Virginia Board for Contractors
facts.fact: Virginia's Board for Contractors also issues individual tradesman licenses (such as journeyman and master) for electricians, plumbers, HVAC tradesmen and gas fitters. These licenses expire three years from the last day of the month issued.

To renew a Virginia tradesman license, plumbing, electrical and HVAC tradesmen need 3 hours of board-approved continuing education on building code changes for each designation per renewal cycle; gas fitter licenses need 1 hour.

facts.source: Va. Code § 43-4
facts.fact: A Virginia mechanics' lien memorandum must be recorded within 90 days from the last day of the month in which the claimant last performed labor or furnished materials, and in no event later than 90 days after the structure is completed or work otherwise ends.

facts.source: Va. Code § 43-4
facts.fact: A Virginia lien memorandum cannot include amounts for labor or materials provided more than 150 days before the last day of work, except that retainage of up to 10% of the total contract price may be included regardless of when the work was done.

facts.source: Va. Code § 43-17
facts.fact: A suit to enforce a Virginia mechanics' lien must be filed within 6 months after the memorandum was recorded or within 60 days after the building is completed or work otherwise ends, whichever is later.

facts.source: Va. Code § 11-4.6
facts.fact: Under Virginia's private construction prompt pay law, an owner must pay a general contractor within 60 days of receiving an invoice for satisfactorily completed work (or give written notice of withholding within 45 days), and the general contractor must pay a subcontractor by the earlier of 60 days after the sub's invoice or 7 days after receiving the owner's payment. Late payments carry interest penalties consistent with § 2.2-4355.

facts.source: RCW 18.27; Washington Department of Labor & Industries (L&I), Register as a Contractor page
facts.fact: Washington contractors must register with the Department of Labor & Industries (L&I) as either a general contractor (may do most types of work and hire subcontractors) or a specialty contractor (limited to one of 63 specialties and may not hire subcontractors). Basic contractor registration requires no exam.

facts.source: RCW 18.27.040; Washington L&I, Register as a Contractor page
facts.fact: Since July 1, 2024, Washington general contractors must post a $30,000 continuous surety bond (or assigned savings account) and specialty contractors a $15,000 bond. A general contractor who switches to specialty cannot lower the bond for 2 years.

facts.source: RCW 18.27.050; Washington L&I, Register as a Contractor page
facts.fact: Washington registered contractors must carry general liability insurance of either $200,000 public liability plus $50,000 property damage, or $250,000 combined single limit.
A Washington contractor certificate of registration is valid for two years and must be renewed on or before its expiration date with the fee and proof of bond and liability insurance.

An unregistered contractor in Washington cannot bring or maintain a lawsuit to collect compensation for contracting work or for breach of contract unless it proves it was a duly registered contractor.

A Washington journey level electrician certificate generally requires an approved 8,000-hour apprenticeship with at least 4,000 hours of new industrial or commercial installations. Residential and most specialty electricians need at least 4,000 supervised hours, and a master journey level electrician must have held a journey level certificate for 4 years.

facts.source: RCW 18.106.030; Washington L&I
facts.fact: Washington plumbers must hold an L&I certificate of competency, issued as journey level, specialty or residential service plumber, based on proven experience or an accredited course of study and an exam. Plumbing and electrical work have their own licensing separate from contractor registration.

In Washington, suppliers and others not contracting directly with the owner or prime contractor must give the owner a pre-claim notice of their right to lien. The notice protects only materials or services provided from 60 days before the notice was mailed or delivered (10 days for new single-family residence construction).

A Washington lien claim must be recorded within 90 days after the claimant last furnished labor or materials, and a copy must be given to the owner within 14 days after the claim is filed for recording.

A Washington lien expires 8 calendar months after it is recorded unless an action to foreclose is filed in superior court in that county within that time, and the owner must be served within 90 days after the action is filed.

facts.source: W. Va. Code § 30-42-3(d) (West Virginia Contractor Licensing Act); West Virginia Contractor Licensing Board
facts.fact: West Virginia requires a contractor license from the West Virginia Contractor Licensing Board when the cost of the undertaking is $5,000 or more for residential work or $25,000 or more for commercial work. The board's law moved from Chapter 21, Article 11 to Chapter 30, Article 42 effective June 15, 2021.
facts.note: Current code text https://code.wvlegislature.gov/30-42-3/ (bill history lists 2021 HB2006, 2025 SB871 and 2026 SB65; the split residential/commercial thresholds appear to be recent, so older materials citing a single $2,500 threshold are outdated). Board history https://labor.wv.gov/Licensing/Contractor_License

facts.source: PSI West Virginia Contractor Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 10/5/2023); W. Va. Code § 30-42-7(b)
facts.fact: No West Virginia contractor license is issued without an exam. The PSI Business and Law exam has 50 questions and requires 35 correct (70%); it is open book using the NASCLA Contractors Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, West Virginia 1st Edition (2022).
keywords: West Virginia business and law exam

facts.source: PSI West Virginia Contractor Licensing Board Candidate Information Bulletin (revised 10/5/2023)
facts.fact: West Virginia trade exams through PSI are open book with a 70% passing score: General Building 80 questions (56 correct, mainly IBC), Residential 80 questions (56 correct, mainly IRC), Electrical Contractor 75 questions (53 correct, NEC 2017/2020), Plumbing Contractor 100 questions (70 correct, IPC) and HVAC Contractor 80 questions (56 correct, IMC).
facts.note: https://test-takers.psiexams.com/api/content/bulletin/10551 . Code editions listed (IBC/IRC 2015/2018) may be updated in newer bulletins.

facts.source: W. Va. Code § 30-42-8(a)
facts.fact: A West Virginia contractor license is valid for one year from the date it is issued, so it must be renewed annually.

In West Virginia, a building permit cannot be issued unless the applicant shows a valid contractor license or files an affidavit that licensing does not apply, and licensees must use a signed written contract describing the work and cost for any job of $10,000 or more (materials and labor).

facts.source: West Virginia Division of Labor, Contractor License page
facts.fact: West Virginia contractors must register with the State Tax Department, verify workers' compensation and unemployment coverage where applicable, and comply with wage bonding requirements.

facts.source: W. Va. Code § 21-14-3; W. Va. Code § 29-3B-3
facts.fact: Since January 1, 2009, anyone performing plumbing work in West Virginia must hold a license from the Commissioner of Labor and carry a copy on the job. Electricians are licensed separately under Article 29-3B (journeyman, master and specialty licenses), with rules proposed by the State Fire Marshal.

In West Virginia, a general contractor must record its notice of mechanics' lien within 100 days after completing the work under its contract. A subcontractor must serve notice on the owner and record it with the county commission clerk within 100 days after completing its subcontract.

facts.source: W. Va. Code § 38-2-34
facts.fact: A suit to enforce a West Virginia mechanics' lien must be filed in circuit court within 6 months after the lien notice is filed with the clerk, or the lien is extinguished.

facts.source: Wis. Stat. § 101.654; Wis. Admin. Code ch. SPS 305; Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services (DSPS), Dwelling Contractor Qualifier page
facts.fact: Wisconsin has no general contractor license, but no one may obtain a building permit for a one- or two-family dwelling unless the business holds a Dwelling Contractor (or Dwelling Contractor Restricted) certification from DSPS and employs a certified Dwelling Contractor Qualifier. Owners who live in, or will live in, the home are exempt when pulling their own permit.

facts.source: Wisconsin DSPS, Dwelling Contractor page; Wis. Admin. Code SPS 305
facts.fact: To hold Wisconsin Dwelling Contractor certification, the business must show financial responsibility through either a surety bond of at least $25,000 or general liability insurance of at least $250,000 per occurrence, and must upload current proof at each renewal.

facts.source: Wisconsin DSPS, Dwelling Contractor Qualifier page
facts.fact: A Wisconsin Dwelling Contractor Qualifier certification renews every 2 years and requires 12 hours of department-approved continuing education, including 4 hours on construction laws and codes, contracts, liability and risk management.

facts.source: Wis. Admin. Code SPS 305 (Dwelling Contractor Qualifier)
facts.fact: To become a Wisconsin Dwelling Contractor Qualifier, an applicant completes a 12-hour DSPS-approved initial education course rather than passing a state exam.
facts.note: Commonly stated requirement, but the DSPS qualifier page reviewed this session did not show the initial course hours and the SPS 305 text could not be retrieved; confirm with DSPS.

facts.source: Wisconsin DSPS, Master Electrician page; Wis. Admin. Code SPS 305.07
facts.fact: Wisconsin electricians are credentialed by DSPS. Renewal of a master electrician license requires at least 24 hours of acceptable continuing education, entered by the course provider.

On Wisconsin residential projects of four or fewer units, a prime contractor that uses subcontractors or suppliers must give the owner a lien notice, either in the written contract or served within 10 days after first furnishing labor or materials. Subcontractors and suppliers must serve their own notice of right to lien within 60 days after first furnishing.
facts.note: From secondary sources (law firm article https://www.boardmanclark.com/publications/business-minute/prime-contractor-lien-guidelines-for-wisconsin-residential-small-projects-private-small-projects and https://www.siteline.com/mechanics-lien-rights/wisconsin ); the Wisconsin statutes site blocked automated access.

facts.source: Wis. Stat. § 779.06
facts.fact: In Wisconsin, a lien claimant must give the owner a written notice of intent to file a lien at least 30 days before filing, and must file the lien claim with the clerk of circuit court within 6 months after last furnishing labor or materials. An action to enforce must be filed within 2 years after the lien claim is filed.
facts.note: From a law firm summary dated 2018 https://www.boardmanclark.com/publications/business-minute/prime-contractor-lien-guidelines-for-wisconsin-residential-small-projects-private-small-projects ; statute text not retrievable this session.

facts.source: Wyoming licensing structure (secondary guides); local building departments
facts.fact: Wyoming has no statewide general contractor, plumbing or HVAC license; those are licensed by cities and counties (for example Cheyenne and Casper). Electrical work is the main construction trade licensed statewide, through the Wyoming State Fire Marshal's Electrical Safety program.
facts.note: Reported consistently by licensing guides; electrical licensing confirmed on https://wsfm.wyo.gov/electrical-safety/licensing , but no official page explicitly stating the absence of state GC/plumbing/HVAC licenses was retrieved.

facts.source: Wyoming State Fire Marshal, Electrical Safety Licensing page; W.S. Title 35, Ch. 9
facts.fact: A Wyoming journeyman electrician exam requires 4 years (8,000 hours) of experience plus 576 hours of approved classroom instruction (144 per year). The master exam requires 8 years (16,000 hours), including 4 years (8,000 hours) as a licensed journeyman, plus the 576 classroom hours. Apprentices must begin licensing within 10 days of starting employment.

facts.source: Wyoming State Fire Marshal, Electrical Safety Licensing page
facts.fact: A Wyoming electrical contractor license must have a Wyoming-licensed master electrician as qualifier (master of record), and electrical contractor licenses expire on July 1 following the date of issue. A licensed journeyman or master may supervise no more than two apprentices at a time.

facts.source: Wyoming State Fire Marshal, Electrical Safety Licensing page
facts.fact: Wyoming electrical exams are based on the currently adopted National Electrical Code. Reciprocity exempts an applicant only from the exam (not other licensing requirements) and requires the prior exam score to be at least 70% for journeyman or 75% for master, with the license held at least 1 year.

facts.source: Wyoming State Fire Marshal, Electrical Safety Licensing page
facts.fact: Wyoming journeyman and master electrician licenses are valid for 3 years, and renewal requires at least 16 hours of board-approved update education during the license period, with at least 8 hours on the National Electrical Code.

In Wyoming, a contractor must send the owner a preliminary notice of lien rights before receiving any payment (including advances), and subcontractors and suppliers must send it within 30 days after first providing services or materials. Failing to send the notice on time bars the right to a lien.

A Wyoming contractor must file its lien statement within 150 days, and subcontractors and other claimants within 120 days, measured from the earlier of the last day of work or materials or substantial completion. Written notice of intent to file must be sent to the record owner at least 20 days before filing.
An action to foreclose a Wyoming construction lien must be started within 180 days after the lien statement is filed.
